message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This evaluation gives the University the evidence it has been asking for on continuation. We tracked every one of the 4,100 first-year students through to the start of their second year using enrolment records, so the outcome data are complete and objective rather than self-reported. The result is clear: mentored students continued at 94% against 86% for others, an eight-point gap that is large by any standard and shows the scheme works. The financial case follows directly. Those 99 or so additional continuing students are worth around £1.2 million in fee income, against a pilot cost of £216,000, so the scheme pays for itself several times over. The qualitative feedback, with a 4.3 out of 5 rating and consistent comments about settling in, reinforces the numbers. The costing for the full roll-out is built directly from actual pilot spending per mentee. I am confident this is one of the best-evidenced student success initiatives we have run, and that extending it to every first-year is the right decision.
</author>

<document>
Evaluation of the First-Year Peer Mentoring Scheme, 2025-26
Student Success Unit, Northbridge University, July 2026

1. Purpose
Continuation from first to second year is a key regulatory and financial measure for the University. In 2024-25, 13% of full-time first-year undergraduates did not continue into their second year. In 2025-26 the University piloted a peer mentoring scheme for first-year students. This report evaluates the pilot and recommends whether it should be extended.

2. The scheme
Students in their second or third year were recruited and trained as mentors, and each was matched with up to eight first-year mentees from the same faculty. Mentors held a group session every fortnight during the first term and were available for one-to-one meetings throughout the year. Mentors were paid £1,200 for the year. They attended a half-day training session in September covering listening skills, signposting to support services and safeguarding, and were supported by a coordinator in each faculty. First-year students were invited to opt in during welcome week.

Recruiting mentors proved harder than expected. We advertised 200 mentor posts and filled 155, which allowed us to offer places to 1,240 first-year students (155 mentors with eight mentees each). Mentee places were taken up within the first two weeks and a waiting list was closed at 300 names.

3. Who took part
Of the 4,100 full-time first-year students, 1,240 took part. Mentees were more likely than other first-years to be living in university halls (78% compared with 52%) and were somewhat more likely to have entered with higher tariff qualifications. They were similar to non-mentees in age and gender.

4. Results
Table 1. Continuation into second year, 2025-26 entrants
Group | Students | Continuing to year two | Continuation rate
Mentored | 1,240 | 1,166 | 94.0%
Not mentored | 2,860 | 2,460 | 86.0%
All first-years | 4,100 | 3,626 | 88.4%

Mentored students were eight percentage points more likely to continue into their second year. Overall continuation rose to 88.4%, from 87% the previous year.

The eight-point gap is clear evidence that peer mentoring improves continuation. Applied to the 1,240 mentees, it means that around 99 students continued who would otherwise have left. At £9,250 a year in tuition fee income, these students are worth about £1.2 million to the University in their second year alone.

Mentees rated the scheme 4.3 out of 5 in the end-of-year survey, and many commented that it helped them settle in and find out about support services. Mentors reported that the role improved their own confidence and employability.

5. Costs
The pilot cost £186,000 for mentor pay, £12,000 for training and £18,000 for coordination, a total of £216,000, or about £174 per mentee.

6. Recommendation
We recommend that from 2026-27 peer mentoring becomes a standard part of the first-year experience, with every full-time first-year student allocated a mentor automatically rather than opting in. On the pilot's costs of about £174 per mentee, this would cost around £714,000 a year for 4,100 students. On the pilot's results, it would raise continuation to around 94% across the whole first-year cohort, a gain of over 200 continuing students a year, and the fee income retained would cover the cost several times over.

7. Conclusion
The pilot has shown that peer mentoring improves continuation by eight percentage points, pays for itself many times over, and is valued by mentees and mentors alike. Extending it to all first-year students is a clear opportunity to improve outcomes and secure the University's continuation performance.
</document>
response:
# Review: First-Year Peer Mentoring Evaluation

**Verdict:** The recommendation may still turn out to be right, but this evaluation doesn't show it. The author's summary is considerably more confident than the document supports. The outcome data may be solid, but the comparison, the financial case and the roll-out costing all have problems.

## Main problems

**1. The 8-point gap is not evidence that the scheme works (selection bias).**
- Students opted in, and places went first-come, first-served within about two weeks. Mentees are therefore likely to be the more motivated and engaged students.
- The report itself shows that mentees differ on factors linked to continuation. 78% lived in halls versus 52%, and they were somewhat more likely to have higher entry tariffs.
- Faculty mix isn't reported either, and continuation varies by subject.
- The author's point that the data are "complete and objective" answers a measurement question. The weakness here is the comparison group, not the measurement.
- Sampling noise isn't the issue. With these group sizes the gap is statistically precise (roughly ±2 points). The problem is bias, not chance.

**2. The report's own numbers suggest the effect is overstated.**
- If 99 students really were retained by the scheme, overall continuation should have risen by about 2.4 points. It rose from 87% to 88.4%, about 1.4 points, or roughly 57 students.
- Removing the 99 would also put the 2025-26 cohort at about 86%, below last year's 87%. This is consistent with the stronger, more engaged students having opted in and left a weaker comparison group behind.

**3. The £1.2 million figure is an arithmetic error.**
- 99 × £9,250 is about £916,000, not £1.2 million.
- This also assumes the whole gap is causal, and that gross fee income is the right measure rather than income net of the cost of teaching those students.

**4. The roll-out costing doesn't scale.**
- £174 per mentee comes from an 8:1 ratio and a mentor pool that was hard to fill. Only 155 of 200 posts were filled, which the report acknowledges.
- Covering 4,100 students at 8:1 needs about 513 mentors, more than three times the pilot's number. There is no evidence that many second- and third-year students would come forward at £1,200, and pay or ratios might have to change.
- Training and coordination costs may not scale linearly either.
- The claim that the costing is "built directly from actual pilot spending per mentee" is true, but it ignores this constraint.

**5. The projection to 94% across the whole cohort is unsupported.**
- It assumes the effect carries over to students who didn't opt in, and who are probably less engaged and less likely to use a mentor.
- Moving from opt-in to automatic allocation changes the intervention, not just its size.
- The "over 200 additional students" and the "several times over" payback both rest on this assumption.

**6. Timing needs checking.**
- The report is dated July 2026, but the author says outcomes were taken from enrolment records at the start of the second year, which would be September or October.
- Please confirm what "continuing" actually means here. It may be re-enrolment intentions, or status at a cut-off date. This affects how complete the data really are.

**7. The satisfaction evidence is weaker than presented.**
- The 4.3/5 rating comes from an end-of-year survey. Students who withdrew, the very group the scheme targets, are unlikely to have answered it.
- No response rate is given, and satisfaction ratings say nothing about whether mentoring caused continuation.

## What holds up
- The table arithmetic is internally consistent (1,166 + 2,460 = 3,626, and the percentages are correct).
- The cost arithmetic checks out (155 × £1,200 = £186,000, and £216,000 ÷ 1,240 ≈ £174).
- Being open about the mentee profile and the recruitment difficulty is to the authors' credit.

## A useful point in the scheme's favour
Break-even is a low bar. Retaining about 23 students (roughly 1.9 points among mentees) would cover the pilot cost at £9,250 each. The roll-out would need about 77 students, also roughly 1.9 points. So even if only a fraction of the gap is causal, the scheme could still pay for itself. The report should make this argument instead of claiming the full gap as proven.

## Suggested fixes
1. Compare mentees with the 300 students on the waiting list, who wanted mentoring but didn't get it. This is the best available comparison group.
2. Run a regression or matching analysis controlling for halls residence, tariff, faculty, age, gender and similar factors, and report the adjusted gap with a confidence interval.
3. Correct the £1.2 million figure, and present benefits as a range based on the share of the gap that is causal.
4. Re-cost the roll-out with the mentor numbers required, a realistic recruitment and pay scenario, and non-linear coordination and training costs.
5. Consider a phased roll-out, or randomised allocation of places when demand exceeds supply, so that next year's evidence is stronger.
6. Clarify the continuation definition and data date, and report the survey response rate.
7. Tone down "shows the scheme works," "best-evidenced" and "pays for itself many times over" to match what the analysis supports.
